segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In my first account, Theophilus, I wrote about everything that Jesus began to do and to teach

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: until the day he was taken up, after he had given instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles he had chosen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To them he also presented himself alive after his suffering by many convincing proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And while eating with them, he ordered them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Father,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “which you heard from me;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when they had come together, they asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, are you restoring the kingdom to Israel at this time?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has set by his own authority,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After he said this, as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as they were gazing into heaven while he was going, suddenly two men in white clothes were standing beside them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they returned to Jerusalem from what is called the Mount of Olives, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had entered the city, they went up to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All these were devoting themselves with one mind to prayer, together with some women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days Peter stood up among the brothers and sisters (the crowd of people gathered together was about one hundred twenty) and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David about Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this service.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (Now this man acquired a field with the wages of his wrongdoing, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It became known to all who lived in Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one living in it,’ and, ‘Let another take his position as overseer.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So, of the men who accompanied us during the whole time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: beginning from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they put forward two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also known as Justus, and Matthias.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they prayed and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: to take the place in this service and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles.

notes.traditional: the former treatise; the first book
notes.note: The reference is to the Gospel of Luke, which is addressed to the same Theophilus and which Acts continues. The Greek word was a normal term for one volume of a longer work.

notes.traditional: being assembled together with them; while staying with them
notes.note: The Greek verb is rare and its sense here is disputed. It may mean “eating with,” “gathering together with,” or, as a spelling variant of a similar verb, “staying with.” “Eating with” has ancient support and fits Luke’s emphasis elsewhere that the risen Jesus ate with his disciples (Luke 24:41–43; Acts 10:41), but many translations choose one of the other options.

This is how Luke describes angels: the “two men in dazzling clothes” at the tomb in Luke 24:4 are called angels in Luke 24:23, and Acts 10 describes the same figure both as an angel and as a man in bright clothing. Their words here are therefore marked as angelic speech, though the text itself says only “men.”

This was the distance Jewish tradition allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath without breaking the rest, reckoned at two thousand cubits, a little over half a mile or about one kilometer. Luke uses it simply as a measure of distance.

The word means someone zealous or fervently devoted, often for God’s law. Whether it marks Simon as a member of a revolutionary movement is uncertain, since an organized party called the Zealots is clearly attested only some decades later, around the war with Rome. The epithet may simply describe his religious fervor.

The Greek says only “Judas of James.” This construction normally names a father, as it does for “James of Alphaeus” in the same list, and most modern translations render it “son of James.” The King James Version took it as “brother,” identifying him with the Jude of Jude 1.

The Greek plural was the ordinary way to refer to a mixed group of siblings or fellow members of a community, and the group here includes the women of verse 14. Many translations keep “brothers,” and some use “believers.” In verse 16 Peter’s address adds the word for “men,” a formal way of opening a speech, and is rendered “Brothers.”

Most translations have “ministry” here. In the first century the word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession, so “service,” a standard lexicon gloss, is used throughout this translation.

notes.phrase: Now this man acquired a field
notes.note: Verses 18 and 19 are set off here as an aside by the narrator, not as part of Peter’s speech. This is the view of most modern editors and translations. Peter would hardly need to tell residents of Jerusalem what was known to all Jerusalem or to translate a word from “their own language.” Some translations nevertheless leave the verses within the speech.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a worker’s pay, and here it refers to the money Judas was paid for betraying Jesus. English translations vary among “reward,” “wages” and “payment.” “Wages” is used in this translation wherever the phrase “wages of wrongdoing” occurs.

The Greek phrase normally means “becoming prone,” that is, falling face down. A minority of scholars, following some ancient interpreters, take it as “swelling up.” Matthew 27:3–10 gives a different account, in which Judas hangs himself and the priests buy the field. How the two accounts relate is debated.

notes.phrase: it is written in the book of Psalms
notes.note: The two quotations are from Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8, in the wording of the Greek translation of the Psalms. Both psalms are prayers of a righteous sufferer against his enemies. The first is plural in the psalm (“their”) and is applied here in the singular to Judas.

candidates.rendering: brothers (siblings, v. 14); brothers and sisters (community, v. 15); Brothers (address with ἄνδρες, v. 16)
candidates.reason: The community sense occurs hundreds of times across Acts and the letters, and translators split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers,” so readers need one policy.
A favorite word in Acts (also Romans 15:6) rendered variously as “with one accord,” “together,” “unanimously” or “with one mind,” and the repetition is thematic.
The construction with ἐν or the bare dative for water and Spirit recurs in all four Gospels, Acts and 1 Corinthians 12:13, and “with” versus “in” should be decided once.
As the term for Jesus’ ascension it recurs in Mark 16:19, Acts 1:2, 1:11, 1:22 and 1 Timothy 3:16, where translations vary among “taken up,” “received up” and “ascended.”
The word means an overseer’s office here and in 1 Timothy 3:1 but “visitation” in Luke 19:44 and 1 Peter 2:12, and the office sense should match the rendering chosen for ἐπίσκοπος.
